We developed a new open-source software package, RevBayes, to address these problems. RevBayes is entirely based on probabilistic graphical models, a powerful generic framework for specifying and analyzing statistical models. Phylogenetic-graphical models can be speciﬁed interactively in RevBayes, piece by piece, using a new succinct and intuitive language called Rev. Rev is similar to the R language and the BUGS model-speciﬁcation language, and should be easy to learn for most users. The strength of RevBayes is the simplicity with which one can design, specify, and implement new and complex models. Fortunately, this tremendous ﬂexibility does not come at the cost of slower computation; as we demonstrate, RevBayes outperforms competing software for several standard analyses. Compared with other programs, RevBayes has fewer black-box elements. Users need to explicitly specify each part of the model and analysis. Although this explicitness may initially be unfamiliar, we are convinced that this transparency will improve understanding of phylogenetic models in our ﬁeld. Moreover, it will motivate the search for improvements to existing methods by brazenly exposing the model choices that we make to critical scrutiny. RevBayes is freely available at http://www.RevBayes.com [Bayesian inference; Graphical models; MCMC; statistical phylogenetics.].

papers.title: Inference and learning in probabilistic logic programs using weighted Boolean formulas
papers.abstract: Abstract Probabilistic logic programs are logic programs in which some of the facts are annotated with probabilities. This paper investigates how classical inference and learning tasks known from the graphical model community can be tackled for probabilistic logic programs. Several such tasks, such as computing the marginals, given evidence and learning from (partial) interpretations, have not really been addressed for probabilistic logic programs before. The first contribution of this paper is a suite of efficient algorithms for various inference tasks. It is based on the conversion of the program and the queries and evidence to a weighted Boolean formula. This allows us to reduce inference tasks to well-studied tasks, such as weighted model counting, which can be solved using state-of-the-art methods known from the graphical model and knowledge compilation literature. The second contribution is an algorithm for parameter estimation in the learning from interpretations setting. The algorithm employs expectation-maximization, and is built on top of the developed inference algorithms. The proposed approach is experimentally evaluated. The results show that the inference algorithms improve upon the state of the art in probabilistic logic programming, and that it is indeed possible to learn the parameters of a probabilistic logic program from interpretations.
papers.venue: Theory and Practice of Logic Programming

papers.title: Approaching the Symbol Grounding Problem with Probabilistic Graphical Models
papers.abstract: In order for robots to engage in dialogue with human teammates, they must have the ability to identify correspondences between elements of language and aspects of the external world. A solution to this symbol‐grounding problem (Harnad, 1990) would enable a robot to interpret commands such as “Drive over to receiving and pick up the tire pallet.” This article describes several of our results that use probabilistic inference to address the symbol‐grounding problem. Our approach is to develop models that factor according to the linguistic structure of a command. We first describe an early result, a generative model that factors according to the sequential structure of language, and then discuss our new framework, generalized grounding graphs (G3). The G3 framework dynamically instantiates a probabilistic graphical model for a natural language input, enabling a mapping between words in language and concrete objects, places, paths, and events in the external world. We report on corpus‐based experiments in which the robot is able to learn and use word meanings in three real‐world tasks: indoor navigation, spatial language video retrieval, and mobile manipulation.
papers.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence

papers.title: Composing graphical models with neural networks for structured representations and fast inference
papers.abstract: We propose a general modeling and inference framework that composes probabilistic graphical models with deep learning methods and combines their respective strengths. Our model family augments graphical structure in latent variables with neural network observation models. For inference, we extend variational autoencoders to use graphical model approximating distributions with recognition networks that output conjugate potentials. All components of these models are learned simultaneously with a single objective, giving a scalable algorithm that leverages stochastic variational inference, natural gradients, graphical model message passing, and the reparameterization trick. We illustrate this framework with several example models and an application to mouse behavioral phenotyping.

papers.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models Based on Spatial Data Structures
papers.abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to enhancing the efficiency of probabilistic graphical model inference by leveraging spatial data structures. Traditional probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) often struggle with scalability when dealing with large spatial datasets, leading to computationally expensive inference processes. This research proposes a framework that integrates PGMs with spatial indexing structures, such as k-d trees and R-trees, to significantly accelerate inference speed. The core idea is to utilize the spatial locality inherent in the data to reduce the search space for nodes during probabilistic reasoning. The proposed method offers a practical solution for modeling and reasoning about spatial data, opening up opportunities for applications in areas like environmental modeling, urban planning, and anomaly detection. This paper details the theoretical foundations, the proposed integration mechanism, and discusses the potential performance gains compared to traditional approaches.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: NEM-Tar: A Probabilistic Graphical Model for Cancer Regulatory Network Inference and Prioritization of Potential Therapeutic Targets From Multi-Omics Data
papers.abstract: Targeted therapy has been widely adopted as an effective treatment strategy to battle against cancer. However, cancers are not single disease entities, but comprising multiple molecularly distinct subtypes, and the heterogeneity nature prevents precise selection of patients for optimized therapy. Dissecting cancer subtype-specific signaling pathways is crucial to pinpointing dysregulated genes for the prioritization of novel therapeutic targets. Nested effects models (NEMs) are a group of graphical models that encode subset relations between observed downstream effects under perturbations to upstream signaling genes, providing a prototype for mapping the inner workings of the cell. In this study, we developed NEM-Tar, which extends the original NEMs to predict drug targets by incorporating causal information of (epi)genetic aberrations for signaling pathway inference. An information theory-based score, weighted information gain (WIG), was proposed to assess the impact of signaling genes on a specific downstream biological process of interest. Subsequently, we conducted simulation studies to compare three inference methods and found that the greedy hill-climbing algorithm demonstrated the highest accuracy and robustness to noise. Furthermore, two case studies were conducted using multi-omics data for colorectal cancer (CRC) and gastric cancer (GC) in the TCGA database. Using NEM-Tar, we inferred signaling networks driving the poor-prognosis subtypes of CRC and GC, respectively. Our model prioritized not only potential individual drug targets such as HER2, for which FDA-approved inhibitors are available but also the combinations of multiple targets potentially useful for the design of combination therapies.

papers.title: Probabilistic Graphical Model Representation in Phylogenetics
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen a rapid expansion of the model space explored in statistical phylogenetics, emphasizing the need for new approaches to statistical model representation and software development. Clear communication and representation of the chosen model is crucial for: (i) reproducibility of an analysis, (ii) model development, and (iii) software design. Moreover, a unified, clear and understandable framework for model representation lowers the barrier for beginners and nonspecialists to grasp complex phylogenetic models, including their assumptions and parameter/variable dependencies. Graphical modeling is a unifying framework that has gained in popularity in the statistical literature in recent years. The core idea is to break complex models into conditionally independent distributions. The strength lies in the comprehensibility, flexibility, and adaptability of this formalism, and the large body of computational work based on it. Graphical models are well-suited to teach statistical models, to facilitate communication among phylogeneticists and in the development of generic software for simulation and statistical inference. Here, we provide an introduction to graphical models for phylogeneticists and extend the standard graphical model representation to the realm of phylogenetics. We introduce a new graphical model component, tree plates, to capture the changing structure of the subgraph corresponding to a phylogenetic tree. We describe a range of phylogenetic models using the graphical model framework and introduce modules to simplify the representation of standard components in large and complex models. Phylogenetic model graphs can be readily used in simulation, maximum likelihood inference, and Bayesian inference using, for example, Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs sampling of the posterior distribution.

papers.title: AND/OR search spaces for graphical models
Multi-Marginal Optimal Transport and Probabilistic Graphical Models
papers.abstract: We study multi-marginal optimal transport problems from a probabilistic graphical model perspective. We point out an elegant connection between the two when the underlying cost for optimal transport allows a graph structure. In particular, an entropy regularized multi-marginal optimal transport is equivalent to a Bayesian marginal inference problem for probabilistic graphical models with the additional requirement that some of the marginal distributions are specified. This relation on the one hand extends the optimal transport as well as the probabilistic graphical model theories, and on the other hand leads to fast algorithms for multi-marginal optimal transport by leveraging the well-developed algorithms in Bayesian inference. Several numerical examples are provided to highlight the results.
papers.publisher: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers

papers.title: Graphical models for machine learning and digital communication
Optimal control as a graphical model inference problem
papers.abstract: We reformulate a class of non-linear stochastic optimal control problems introduced by Todorov (in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, vol. 19, pp. 1369–1376, 2007 ) as a Kullback-Leibler (KL) minimization problem. As a result, the optimal control computation reduces to an inference computation and approximate inference methods can be applied to efficiently compute approximate optimal controls. We show how this KL control theory contains the path integral control method as a special case. We provide an example of a block stacking task and a multi-agent cooperative game where we demonstrate how approximate inference can be successfully applied to instances that are too complex for exact computation. We discuss the relation of the KL control approach to other inference approaches to control.

papers.title: Recent Advances in Probabilistic Graphical Models
papers.abstract: Probabilistic graphical models constitute a fundamental tool for the development of intelligent systems.They provide a sound and well-founded approach for performing inference and belief updating in complex domains endowed with uncertainty.A probabilistic graphical model is the result of the combination of a qualitative component (a graph) encoding conditional independence relationships among the variables in the system and a quantitative component consisting of a collection of local probability distributions matching the independence properties specified by the graph.The union of the two components provides a compact representation of the joint probability distribution over the domain being modeled.Bayesian networks are the most prominent type of probabilistic graphical models and have experienced a remarkable methodological development during the past two decades.This has come along with a wide variety of successful applications in different domains.Regardless of the increasing interest in the area, probabilistic graphical models are still facing a number of challenges, covering modeling, inference and learning.This special issue contains seven papers that contribute to the methodological development beyond the current state-of-the-art knowledge.Five of the papers were selected among the contributions presented at the 15th Conference of the Spanish Association of Artificial Intelligence (CAEPIA'2013, Madrid, Spain, September 17-20, 2013).These papers were substantially extended and went through a new and strict review process.The other two papers were invited contributions not presented at the conference and went through the same review process.The first three papers deal with hybrid models, where both discrete and continuous variables coexist.Lucas and Hommersom propose a framework for handling causal independence covering discrete and continuous variables simultaneously.The methodology is based on the convolution concept from probability theory, and the

papers.title: Variational Probabilistic Inference and the QMR-DT Network
papers.abstract: We describe a variational approximation method for efficient inference in large-scale probabilistic models. Variational methods are deterministic procedures that provide approximations to marginal and conditional probabilities of interest. They provide alternatives to approximate inference methods based on stochastic sampling or search. We describe a variational approach to the problem of diagnostic inference in the `Quick Medical Reference' (QMR) network. The QMR network is a large-scale probabilistic graphical model built on statistical and expert knowledge. Exact probabilistic inference is infeasible in this model for all but a small set of cases. We evaluate our variational inference algorithm on a large set of diagnostic test cases, comparing the algorithm to a state-of-the-art stochastic sampling method.

papers.title: Getting Started in Probabilistic Graphical Models
papers.abstract: Probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) have become a popular tool for computational analysis of biological data in a variety of domains. But, what exactly are they and how do they work? How can we use PGMs to discover patterns that are biologically relevant? And to what extent can PGMs help us formulate new hypotheses that are testable at the bench? This note sketches out some answers and illustrates the main ideas behind the statistical approach to biological pattern discovery.

papers.title: GraphPPL.jl: A Probabilistic Programming Language for Graphical Models
papers.abstract: This paper presents GraphPPL.jl, a novel probabilistic programming language designed for graphical models. GraphPPL.jl uniquely represents probabilistic models as factor graphs. A notable feature of GraphPPL.jl is its model nesting capability, which facilitates the creation of modular graphical models and significantly simplifies the development of large (hierarchical) graphical models. Furthermore, GraphPPL.jl offers a plugin system to incorporate inference-specific information into the graph, allowing integration with various well-known inference engines. To demonstrate this, GraphPPL.jl includes a flexible plugin to define a Constrained Bethe Free Energy minimization process, also known as variational inference. In particular, the Constrained Bethe Free Energy defined by GraphPPL.jl serves as a potential inference framework for numerous well-known inference backends, making it a versatile tool for diverse applications. This paper details the design and implementation of GraphPPL.jl, highlighting its power, expressiveness, and user-friendliness. It also emphasizes the clear separation between model definition and inference while providing developers with extensibility and customization options. This establishes GraphPPL.jl as a high-level user interface language that allows users to create complex graphical models without being burdened with the complexity of inference while allowing backend developers to easily adopt GraphPPL.jl as their frontend language.

papers.title: Contextual Symmetries in Probabilistic Graphical Models
papers.abstract: An important approach for efficient inference in probabilistic graphical models exploits symmetries among objects in the domain. Symmetric variables (states) are collapsed into meta-variables (meta-states) and inference algorithms are run over the lifted graphical model instead of the flat one. Our paper extends existing definitions of symmetry by introducing the novel notion of contextual symmetry. Two states that are not globally symmetric, can be contextually symmetric under some specific assignment to a subset of variables, referred to as the context variables. Contextual symmetry subsumes previous symmetry definitions and can rep resent a large class of symmetries not representable earlier. We show how to compute contextual symmetries by reducing it to the problem of graph isomorphism. We extend previous work on exploiting symmetries in the MCMC framework to the case of contextual symmetries. Our experiments on several domains of interest demonstrate that exploiting contextual symmetries can result in significant computational gains.

papers.title: Teaching Probabilistic Graphical Models with OpenMarkov
papers.abstract: OpenMarkov is an open-source software tool for probabilistic graphical models. It has been developed especially for medicine, but has also been used to build applications in other fields and for tuition, in more than 30 countries. In this paper we explain how to use it as a pedagogical tool to teach the main concepts of Bayesian networks and influence diagrams, such as conditional dependence and independence, d-separation, Markov blankets, explaining away, optimal policies, expected utilities, etc., and some inference algorithms: logic sampling, likelihood weighting, and arc reversal. The facilities for learning Bayesian networks interactively can be used to illustrate step by step the performance of the two basic algorithms: search-and-score and PC.

papers.title: Adaptive Probabilistic Graphical Model Learning
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to learning probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) by dynamically adapting their structure based on the underlying data distribution. Traditional PGM learning often relies on pre-defined structures, which may not always capture the intricate relationships present in complex datasets. Our method, Adaptive Probabilistic Graphical Model Learning (APGML), leverages Bayesian inference and variational inference techniques, coupled with gradient descent optimization, to automatically adjust the model's topology – specifically, the nodes and edges – during the learning process. The core claim is that this adaptive approach leads to a more precise representation of the data and improved model accuracy. We introduce a framework that iteratively refines the PGM structure, driven by the data, ultimately resulting in a model that better reflects the underlying dependencies. This work addresses a significant challenge in PGM learning: the selection of an appropriate graph structure – a problem often tackled through manual design or heuristic search algorithms – by allowing the model to evolve based on the observed data. We outline the key components of the APGML algorithm, including the variational inference process, the structural adaptation mechanism, and the optimization strategy.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: A Review on Probabilistic Graphical Models and Tools
papers.abstract: Our daily life is full of challenges, and the biggest challenge is the unpredictability of many of our significant life events. To deal with this unpredictability, analysing the probability of events has become very important. In particular, the theorem of English statistician Thomas Bayes has been revolutionary. Numerous theories and techniques have been proposed, and many tools have been developed to solve real-life problems based on the theorem, yet it is still very much an area of active research. It still attracts researchers dealing with cutting-edge technologies. One tool that has been used extensively in modelling probabilistic analysis for decades is the Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM). PGMs have very challenging childhood but glorious youth. The vast applicability of the models in cutting-edge technologies attracts researchers, modellers and scientists of diversified fields. Hence there are numerous models with their respective features, merits and backlogs. To date, there have been very few surveys conducted among the wide range of models and their associated tools. More specifically, those few reviews are highly application and domain focused, and limited to three to four very popular and widely used models and their associated learning and inference algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first that presents the features, limitations, design and implementation platforms, research challenges and applicability of the models based on a common framework that consists of some essential attributes of the popular PGMs and tools for probabilistic analysis. The study helps deciding an appropriate tool as per the perspective of the application and feature of the tool. This paper concludes with future research scope and a non-exhaustive list of applications of PGMs. DUJASE Vol. 6 (2) 82-93, 2021 (July)
papers.venue: Dhaka University Journal of Applied Science and Engineering

papers.title: Automorphism Groups of Graphical Models and Lifted Variational Inference
papers.abstract: Using the theory of group action, we first introduce the concept of the automorphism group of an exponential family or a graphical model, thus formalizing the general notion of symmetry of a probabilistic model. This automorphism group provides a precise mathematical framework for lifted inference in the general exponential family. Its group action partitions the set of random variables and feature functions into equivalent classes (called orbits) having identical marginals and expectations. Then the inference problem is effectively reduced to that of computing marginals or expectations for each class, thus avoiding the need to deal with each individual variable or feature. We demonstrate the usefulness of this general framework in lifting two classes of variational approximation for maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference: local linear programming (LP) relaxation and local LP relaxation with cycle constraints; the latter yields the first lifted variational inference algorithm that operates on a bound tighter than the local constraints.

papers.title: Graphical Models for Inference with Missing Data
papers.abstract: We address inference problems associated with missing data using causal Bayesian networks to model the data generation process. We show that procedures based on graphical models can overcome limitations of conventional missing data methods and provide meaningful performance guarantees even when data are Missing Not At Random (MNAR). In particular, we identify conditions that guarantee consistent estimation of parameters of interest in broad categories of missing data problems, and derive procedures for implementing this estimation. We derive testable implications for missing data problems in both MAR (Missing At Random) and MNAR categories. Finally, we apply these techniques to develop a suite of algorithms for closed form estimation of Bayesian network parameters.

papers.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models: A Concise Tutorial
papers.abstract: Probabilistic graphical modeling is a branch of machine learning that uses probability distributions to describe the world, make predictions, and support decision-making under uncertainty. Underlying this modeling framework is an elegant body of theory that bridges two mathematical traditions: probability and graph theory. This framework provides compact yet expressive representations of joint probability distributions, yielding powerful generative models for probabilistic reasoning. This tutorial provides a concise introduction to the formalisms, methods, and applications of this modeling framework. After a review of basic probability and graph theory, we explore three dominant themes: (1) the representation of multivariate distributions in the intuitive visual language of graphs, (2) algorithms for learning model parameters and graphical structures from data, and (3) algorithms for inference, both exact and approximate.

papers.title: Structure Learning of Probabilistic Graphical Models: A Comprehensive Survey
papers.abstract: Probabilistic graphical models combine the graph theory and probability theory to give a multivariate statistical modeling. They provide a unified description of uncertainty using probability and complexity using the graphical model. Especially, graphical models provide the following several useful properties: - Graphical models provide a simple and intuitive interpretation of the structures of probabilistic models. On the other hand, they can be used to design and motivate new models. - Graphical models provide additional insights into the properties of the model, including the conditional independence properties. - Complex computations which are required to perform inference and learning in sophisticated models can be expressed in terms of graphical manipulations, in which the underlying mathematical expressions are carried along implicitly. The graphical models have been applied to a large number of fields, including bioinformatics, social science, control theory, image processing, marketing analysis, among others. However, structure learning for graphical models remains an open challenge, since one must cope with a combinatorial search over the space of all possible structures. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of the existing structure learning algorithms.

papers.title: FSPN: A New Class of Probabilistic Graphical Model
papers.abstract: We introduce factorize sum split product networks (FSPNs), a new class of probabilistic graphical models (PGMs). FSPNs are designed to overcome the drawbacks of existing PGMs in terms of estimation accuracy and inference efficiency. Specifically, Bayesian networks (BNs) have low inference speed and performance of tree structured sum product networks(SPNs) significantly degrades in presence of highly correlated variables. FSPNs absorb their advantages by adaptively modeling the joint distribution of variables according to their dependence degree, so that one can simultaneously attain the two desirable goals: high estimation accuracy and fast inference speed. We present efficient probability inference and structure learning algorithms for FSPNs, along with a theoretical analysis and extensive evaluation evidence. Our experimental results on synthetic and benchmark datasets indicate the superiority of FSPN over other PGMs.

papers.title: On probabilistic inference by weighted model counting
A probabilistic graphical model foundation for enabling predictive digital twins at scale
Constraint Processing in Lifted Probabilistic Inference
papers.abstract: First-order probabilistic models combine representational power of first-order logic with graphical models. There is an ongoing effort to design lifted inference algorithms for first-order probabilistic models. We analyze lifted inference from the perspective of constraint processing and, through this viewpoint, we analyze and compare existing approaches and expose their advantages and limitations. Our theoretical results show that the wrong choice of constraint processing method can lead to exponential increase in computational complexity. Our empirical tests confirm the importance of constraint processing in lifted inference. This is the first theoretical and empirical study of constraint processing in lifted inference.

papers.title: Approximate Implication for Probabilistic Graphical Models
papers.abstract: The graphical structure of Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs) represents the conditional independence (CI) relations that hold in the modeled distribution. Every separator in the graph represents a conditional independence relation in the distribution, making them the vehicle through which new conditional independence relations are inferred and verified. The notion of separation in graphs depends on whether the graph is directed (i.e., a Bayesian Network), or undirected (i.e., a Markov Network). The premise of all current systems-of-inference for deriving CIs in PGMs, is that the set of CIs used for the construction of the PGM hold exactly. In practice, algorithms for extracting the structure of PGMs from data discover approximate CIs that do not hold exactly in the distribution. In this paper, we ask how the error in this set propagates to the inferred CIs read off the graphical structure. More precisely, what guarantee can we provide on the inferred CI when the set of CIs that entailed it hold only approximately? It has recently been shown that in the general case, no such guarantee can be provided. In this work, we prove new negative and positive results concerning this problem. We prove that separators in undirected PGMs do not necessarily represent approximate CIs. In other words, no guarantee can be provided for CIs inferred from the structure of undirected graphs. We prove that such a guarantee exists for the set of CIs inferred in directed graphical models, making the d-separation algorithm a sound and complete system for inferring approximate CIs. We also establish improved approximation guarantees for independence relations derived from marginal and saturated CIs.

papers.title: PROBABILISTIC GRAPHICAL MODELS APPLICATIONS IN MEDICAL RESEARCHES
papers.abstract: The use of intelligent systems in medical research and practice has a long history, becoming an essential support tool nowadays. In this paper, we investigated and presented an overview of the Probabilistic Graphical Models, as well as some applications of them in medical research. We explored these approaches because they are widely used for inference in environments of uncertainty, especially for inter-causal reasoning. Such techniques are established as safe and complete inference mechanisms, which motivated our explanation and analysis. The methods investigated are promising for health research. They can be applied to different types of inference problems, especially causal inference, which is very common in the case of diseases, syndromes, and disorders.
papers.publisher: Instituto Federal do Sul de Minas

papers.title: Graphical Models for Extremes
papers.abstract: Summary Conditional independence, graphical models and sparsity are key notions for parsimonious statistical models and for understanding the structural relationships in the data. The theory of multivariate and spatial extremes describes the risk of rare events through asymptotically justified limit models such as max-stable and multivariate Pareto distributions. Statistical modelling in this field has been limited to moderate dimensions so far, partly owing to complicated likelihoods and a lack of understanding of the underlying probabilistic structures. We introduce a general theory of conditional independence for multivariate Pareto distributions that enables the definition of graphical models and sparsity for extremes. A Hammersley–Clifford theorem links this new notion to the factorization of densities of extreme value models on graphs. For the popular class of Hüsler–Reiss distributions we show that, similarly to the Gaussian case, the sparsity pattern of a general extremal graphical model can be read off from suitable inverse covariance matrices. New parametric models can be built in a modular way and statistical inference can be simplified to lower dimensional marginals. We discuss learning of minimum spanning trees and model selection for extremal graph structures, and we illustrate their use with an application to flood risk assessment on the Danube river.
papers.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B (Statistical Methodology)

papers.title: Variational methods for inference and estimation in graphical models
papers.abstract: Graphical models enhance the representational power of probability models through qualitative characterization of their properties. This also leads to greater efficiency in terms of the computational algorithms that empower such representations. The increasing complexity of these models, however, quickly renders exact probabilistic calculations infeasible. We propose a principled framework for approximating graphical models based on variational methods. We develop variational techniques from the perspective that unifies and expands their applicability to graphical models. These methods allow the (recursive) computation of upper and lower bounds on the quantities of interest. Such bounds yield considerably more information than mere approximations and provide an inherent error metric for tailoring the approximations individually to the cases considered. These desirable properties, concomitant to the variational methods, are unlikely to arise as a result of other deterministic or stochas...

papers.title: Causal Discovery with Bayesian Copula Networks
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery utilizing Bayesian Copula Networks (BCNs). Traditional causal discovery methods often struggle with complex dependencies, confounding, and selection bias, leading to inaccurate inferences. BCNs provide a powerful framework for representing and analyzing multivariate data by encoding variables as copulas, capturing their joint distributions. The core of the method lies in learning these copulas and then applying Bayesian inference to estimate causal relationships, explicitly addressing uncertainty. The approach offers a more robust solution, particularly when dealing with intricate dependencies, by leveraging the inherent structure of copulas and the probabilistic reasoning of Bayesian networks. This work outlines the theoretical underpinnings of BCNs, detailing the construction of the network, the learning process, and the inference mechanisms. We demonstrate the potential of this method through a conceptual framework, highlighting its advantages over existing approaches and paving the way for future research and applications.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Bayesian Networks and Causal Discovery
papers.abstract: The discovery of the precise causal representations underlying complex data forms the bedrock of artificial intelligence research [...].

papers.title: Temporal Bayesian Networks with Causal Discovery
papers.abstract: This research introduces a novel approach to temporal data analysis by integrating Temporal Bayesian Networks (TBNs) with causal discovery algorithms. Traditional TBNs primarily focus on modeling temporal dependencies without explicitly considering causal relationships. This limitation hinders their ability to accurately represent and interpret dynamic systems, particularly when causal influences are significant. The proposed method addresses this gap by leveraging Bayesian networks to represent temporal dependencies and employing a causal discovery algorithm to infer the underlying causal structure from observed time series data. The resulting Temporal Bayesian Networks with Causal Discovery (TBCDNs) provide a more robust and informative model of dynamic systems, allowing for the identification of causal influences and facilitating more accurate predictions. This work demonstrates the potential of TBCDNs for applications in various domains where understanding the temporal evolution of systems and their causal relationships is crucial. The core contributions lie in the integration of causal inference within a temporal modeling framework and the development of a methodology for learning causal structures from time series data. The resultant network structure is represented by a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where nodes represent variables and edges represent probabilistic dependencies, incorporating temporal constraints.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Graph-Based Bayesian Networks for Causal Discovery
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to causal discovery leveraging graph-based Bayesian networks. Traditional causal discovery algorithms often encounter difficulties when dealing with intricate graph structures, leading to inaccurate or incomplete causal models. Our method addresses this limitation by integrating Bayesian network principles with graph-based reasoning, allowing for iterative refinement of the graph structure based on observed statistical dependencies while enforcing causal consistency constraints. The core of our approach lies in utilizing algorithms like PC algorithm and its variants to identify conditional dependencies between variables. We introduce a framework that dynamically updates the graph structure, prioritizing connections that align with both statistical dependence and causal assumptions. The resulting Bayesian network provides a more robust and scalable solution for causal inference, particularly in scenarios with high-dimensional data and complex relationships. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis and outlined within the framework of conditional independence tests. Future research directions include exploring hybrid approaches combining this method with reinforcement learning and incorporating domain-specific knowledge to further enhance the accuracy of causal models.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Epistemic Bayesian Networks for Causal Discovery
papers.abstract: Traditional causal discovery methods often assume complete knowledge of the system being studied, a simplifying assumption rarely met in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces Epistemic Bayesian Networks (EBNs), an extension of standard Bayesian Networks that explicitly incorporates the observer's knowledge and uncertainty. EBNs utilize 'epistemic nodes' to represent beliefs about the causal relationships between variables, informed by both prior knowledge and observational data. This approach addresses the limitations of conventional methods by accounting for the observer's subjective perspective, potentially leading to more accurate and robust causal inferences. The core mechanism involves defining and utilizing epistemic nodes within the network structure, with associated probability distributions reflecting the observer's confidence in different relationships. We explore the theoretical foundations of EBNs, outlining key concepts and proposing a framework for constructing and analyzing these networks. This work lays the groundwork for a new paradigm in causal discovery, where the observer's role is central to the process.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Bayesian Network Causal Discovery and Decision Making
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the application of Bayesian Networks (BNs) for both causal discovery and decision-making within complex systems characterized by uncertainty. The core argument is that BNs offer a robust framework for modeling dependencies and inferring causal relationships, ultimately leading to more effective decision-making strategies. We propose a methodology utilizing BNs to identify causal links from observational data and subsequently employ these discovered relationships in a decision-making process. The novelty lies in the integration of BN causal discovery with probabilistic decision theory, providing a unified approach to handling uncertainty and complexity. We present a theoretical framework and discuss key considerations for applying this approach, highlighting its potential advantages over traditional methods. The approach avoids reliance on strong assumptions about data and allows for the representation of intricate dependencies, making it suitable for a wide range of applications. Finally, we demonstrate the conceptual framework and discuss potential future research directions.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Bayesian Network-Based Causal Discovery Algorithm (BNCDA)
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Bayesian Network-Based Causal Discovery Algorithm (BNCDA), a novel approach to causal inference leveraging the structure of Bayesian Networks. The core claim of this work is that Bayesian Networks can be effectively utilized to discover causal relationships within datasets. The algorithm operates by learning conditional independence relationships from data and employing this information to infer a causal graph. Unlike traditional causal discovery methods that heavily rely on domain expertise and prior knowledge, BNCDA aims to learn directly from data. This paper outlines the theoretical foundations of BNCDA, details the algorithm's implementation, and discusses potential applications and limitations. The ultimate goal is to provide a data-driven approach to causal discovery, facilitating more robust and interpretable causal models.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery and Decision-Making Based on Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the application of Bayesian Networks for both causal discovery and decision-making. The core premise is that Bayesian Networks can be leveraged to uncover causal relationships within data, and subsequently integrated with decision theory to facilitate optimal decision-making. We propose a framework that utilizes structure learning algorithms to automatically learn the underlying Bayesian Network structure from data. This learned network is then employed for causal inference through Bayesian reasoning. Finally, this causal understanding is used within a decision-making process to identify the optimal course of action. The novelty of this approach lies in combining these two powerful methodologies, offering a new perspective for complex problem-solving. This work demonstrates a theoretical framework, without empirical validation through experimentation, focused on the conceptual integration of causal discovery and decision-making using Bayesian Networks.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery via Bayesian Inference on Dynamic Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to causal discovery within dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs). The core challenge in inferring causal relationships from time-varying data lies in the complexities introduced by confounding factors and intricate temporal dependencies. This research develops a Bayesian inference framework tailored explicitly for DBNs, incorporating mechanisms to model these temporal aspects and mitigate confounding through a layered strategy combining prior knowledge and data-driven learning. The proposed framework aims to provide a robust and interpretable solution for uncovering causal structures within dynamic systems, addressing a significant gap in current causal discovery methodologies. The key innovations lie in the dynamic updating of the Bayesian network structure and parameters, as well as the integration of techniques for handling spurious correlations. The framework is designed to improve the accuracy and reliability of causal inferences, particularly in scenarios where data is inherently noisy and subject to temporal variations. This work contributes to the field by offering a more principled and effective approach to causal discovery in dynamic environments.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Individualized Causal Discovery with Latent Trajectory Embedded Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: Bayesian networks have been widely used to generate causal hypotheses from multivariate data. Despite their popularity, the vast majority of existing causal discovery approaches make the strong assumption of a (partially) homogeneous sampling scheme. However, such assumption can be seriously violated, causing significant biases when the underlying population is inherently heterogeneous. To this end, we propose a novel causal Bayesian network model, termed BN-LTE, that embeds heterogeneous samples onto a low-dimensional manifold and builds Bayesian networks conditional on the embedding. This new framework allows for more precise network inference by improving the estimation resolution from the population level to the observation level. Moreover, while causal Bayesian networks are in general not identifiable with purely observational, cross-sectional data due to Markov equivalence, with the blessing of causal effect heterogeneity, we prove that the proposed BN-LTE is uniquely identifiable under relatively mild assumptions. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the superior performance of BN-LTE in causal structure learning as well as inferring observation-specific gene regulatory networks from observational data.

papers.title: Causal Discovery and Reasoning for Intrusion Detectionusing Bayesian Network
papers.abstract: Computer security is essential in information technology world today; confidentiality, availability and integrity of data are the aspects concerned.Firewall has been widely deployed as a protection but it is no longer adequate to against the intelligent intrusions and attacks which keep changing and transforming.A network intrusion detection and analysis system has been introduced in this paper to resolve the problems of data confidentiality, availability and integrity.The challenge of the study is; first, to model the network intrusion detection domain and second, to perform causal reasoning for intrusion detection and analysis based on the domain model constructed earlier.In this paper, a methodology has been proposed to resolve the two problems mentioned above.Both problems will be addressed under causal knowledge driven approach where intrusion detection is viewed as fault diagnosis and prognosis processes.We have proposed Bayesian network for the modeling of network intrusion domain.Also, powerful reasoning capabilities of Bayesian network have been applied to discover intrusion attacks.Since the capabilities of causal reasoning using Bayesian network have not been fully discovered in the domain of intrusion detection by most of the researchers before, this research work is to bridge the gap.From the results of the experiment, we have concluded that the capability of Bayesian learning is reasonably accurate and efficient.
papers.venue: International Journal of Machine Learning and Computing

papers.title: Causal Discovery via Bayesian Networks with Hidden Markov Models
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery leveraging the strengths of Bayesian Networks and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). Existing causal discovery algorithms often falter when dealing with complex, time-varying dependencies inherent in many real-world systems. Our method addresses this limitation by integrating Bayesian Network inference with HMMs to explicitly model temporal dynamics and subsequently infer causal relationships from sequential data. The core claim is that by incorporating temporal structure, we achieve a more robust and accurate understanding of causal dependencies. We present a framework for constructing Bayesian Networks augmented with HMMs, detailing the inference process and outlining the key steps involved in discovering causal relationships from time-series data. The proposed method offers a significant advancement in causal discovery, particularly for systems exhibiting temporal evolution and intricate dependencies. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline, paving the way for future empirical validation.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery via Bayesian Networks with Dynamic Structure Learning
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to causal discovery utilizing Bayesian Networks and dynamic structure learning. Traditional Bayesian Network structure learning algorithms are static, failing to account for evolving causal relationships observed in time-series data. This research addresses this limitation by extending these algorithms to incorporate temporal dynamics. The core claim is that causal discovery can be significantly improved by explicitly modeling how relationships change over time. The proposed mechanism involves adapting Bayesian Network structure learning algorithms to handle time-series data, enabling the network structure to dynamically adjust to shifts in the underlying causal dependencies. This approach offers a more realistic representation of complex systems where causal relationships are not fixed but evolve with time. The paper details the theoretical framework, outlines a proposed methodology, and discusses potential challenges and future research directions. We demonstrate the potential for increased accuracy and robustness in causal inference by incorporating temporal information.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Exact discovery is polynomial for certain sparse causal Bayesian networks
papers.abstract: Causal Bayesian networks are widely used tools for summarising the dependencies between variables and elucidating their putative causal relationships. By restricting the search to trees, for example, learning the optimum from data is polynomial, but this does not guarantee finding the optimal network overall. Without similar restrictions, exact discovery of the optimum is computationally hard in general and no polynomial results are known. The current state-of-the-art approaches are integer linear programming over the underlying space of directed acyclic graphs, dynamic programming and shortest-path searches over the space of topological orders, and constraint programming combining both. For dynamic programming over orders, the computational complexity is known to be exponential base 2 in the number of variables in the network. We demonstrate how to use properties of Bayesian networks to prune the search space and lower the computational cost, while still guaranteeing exact discovery of the provably optimal network. We also include new path-search and divide-and-conquer criteria. Without a priori constraining the search to certain types of networks, the algorithm completes in quadratic time when the optimum is a matching, and in polynomial time when the optimum belongs to any network class with logarithmically-bound largest connected components. In simulation studies we observe the polynomial dependence for sparse networks and that, beyond some critical value, the logarithm of the base grows with the network density. Our approach then out-competes the state-of-the-art at lower densities. These results therefore pave the way for faster exact causal discovery in larger and sparser networks.

papers.title: Causal Discovery via Bayesian Episodic Memory Networks
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to causal discovery leveraging the principles of episodic memory networks and Bayesian inference. The core idea is that episodic memory networks, representing states and causal transitions, can be effectively utilized for causal discovery, particularly within partially observable environments. We construct these networks, where nodes represent states and edges represent causal relationships, and then employ Bayesian inference to estimate the conditional probability distributions associated with each state. This allows us to identify causal relationships by simulating interventions and observations, thereby enhancing the robustness and accuracy of the discovery process. The combination of episodic memory and Bayesian causal inference offers a significantly improved method compared to traditional approaches, addressing limitations in environments with incomplete information. This research provides a framework for discovering causal relationships in complex systems where observational data is inherently noisy and partial. The methodology is presented with detailed mathematical formulations, focusing on the core concepts and their application.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Adaptive Bayesian Networks for Causal Discovery with Symbolic Reasoning
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to causal discovery utilizing Adaptive Bayesian Networks (ABNs) coupled with symbolic reasoning. Traditional data-driven causal discovery methods often struggle with spurious correlations and lack interpretability. This work addresses these limitations by integrating domain expertise and logical constraints through a symbolic reasoning engine. The Adaptive Bayesian Network algorithm dynamically adjusts its structure based on both statistical evidence and symbolic knowledge, leading to more accurate and interpretable causal models. The core idea is to augment Bayesian network learning with a mechanism capable of identifying causal relationships based on predefined rules and logical constraints. We introduce a framework where the network's structure evolves adaptively, incorporating symbolic reasoning to resolve ambiguities and guide the discovery process. The resulting ABNs offer improved robustness and interpretability compared to purely data-driven approaches, particularly in domains with rich background knowledge. The algorithm is designed to handle uncertainty effectively, leveraging Bayesian inference and continually updating the network structure based on new observations and symbolic constraints. This research contributes to a more reliable and transparent method for uncovering causal relationships from observational data.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery from Streaming Data with Granger Causality and Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of causal discovery in dynamic environments where data arrives continuously—a scenario often referred to as streaming data. Traditional causal discovery algorithms typically rely on static datasets, rendering them unsuitable for this context. This work proposes a novel algorithm that integrates Granger causality tests with Bayesian networks to perform causal inference in real-time from streaming data. The algorithm leverages Granger causality to identify potential temporal dependencies between variables, followed by Bayesian network construction to refine the inferred causal relationships. The core claim is that dynamic causal inference is possible and can be effectively performed by this method. The core mechanism is the combination of Granger causality and Bayesian networks. This approach provides a pathway for understanding causal relationships in evolving datasets, offering significant improvements over existing methods. The presented algorithm's capability to handle dynamic causal inference in streaming data scenarios makes it a valuable tool for various applications, including anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, and real-time decision-making.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: The Five‐Gene‐Network Data Analysis with Local Causal Discovery Algorithm Using Causal Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: Using microarray experiments, we can model causal relationships of genes measured through mRNA expression levels. To this end, it is desirable to compare experiments of the system under complete interventions of some genes, such as by knock out of some genes, with experiments of the system under no interventions. However, it is expensive and difficult to conduct wet lab experiments of complete interventions of genes in a biological system. Thus, it will be helpful if we can discover promising causal relationships among genes with no interventions or incomplete interventions, such as by applying a treatment that has unknown effects to modeled genes, in order to identify promising genes to perturb in the system that can later be verified in wet laboratories. In this paper we use causal Bayesian networks to implement a causal discovery algorithm-the equivalence local implicit latent variable scoring method (EquLIM)-that identifies promising causal relationships even with a small dataset generated from no or incomplete interventions. We then apply EquLIM to analyze the five-gene-network data and compare EquLIM's predictions with true causal pairwise relationships between the genes.
papers.venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Causal Discovery from Streaming Data with Intervention-Aware Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to causal discovery from streaming data, specifically addressing the challenges posed by interventions. Traditional causal discovery algorithms often fail to accurately infer causal relationships when interventions are actively occurring, leading to biased and inaccurate models. Our method extends Bayesian Networks by incorporating intervention models, enabling the algorithm to learn causal relationships while explicitly accounting for the impact of observed interventions on the data stream. This intervention-aware framework allows for more robust and accurate causal inference in dynamic environments. We formalize this approach with a detailed mathematical description, including the core Bayesian Network structure and the intervention model integration. The proposed method demonstrates improved accuracy compared to existing algorithms when dealing with streaming data influenced by interventions.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Graph-Based Bayesian Networks for Causal Discovery from Observational Data
papers.abstract: Causal discovery from observational data remains a significant challenge in machine learning and statistics. Traditional methods often struggle with scalability, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional datasets and complex relationships between variables. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing graph-based Bayesian networks for efficient causal inference. We propose an iterative algorithm that leverages graph algorithms to refine a causal graph based on observed data. This approach addresses the limitations of previous methods by providing a scalable framework for identifying causal relationships. The core of the method relies on repeatedly updating the graph structure based on conditional independence tests, ultimately converging towards a graph that accurately reflects the underlying causal structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through theoretical analysis and outline its potential for applications in various domains. The key innovation lies in the strategic combination of graph algorithms and Bayesian network principles to achieve robust and scalable causal discovery.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery from Interventional and Observational Data using Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the potential of integrating interventional and observational data to enhance the accuracy and robustness of causal discovery algorithms. Traditional causal discovery methods often rely solely on observational data, which may be biased due to confounding variables or unobserved confounders. This research proposes a novel approach by leveraging Bayesian networks, allowing for the explicit modeling of causal relationships derived from both experimental (interventional) and observational data. The core claim is that combining these data sources can significantly improve the identification of true causal structures. The mechanism involves utilizing Bayesian networks to represent the probabilistic dependencies between variables, incorporating interventions to directly measure causal effects alongside observational measurements. We explore the theoretical underpinnings and discuss the potential benefits and challenges of this integrated approach, highlighting its advantages over existing techniques. We demonstrate that incorporating interventional data can resolve ambiguities and improve the accuracy of discovered causal graphs, particularly in scenarios with complex confounding. The primary contribution of this work is a framework for robust causal discovery that accounts for both the strength and direction of causal influences.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery from Streaming Data with Bayesian Networks and Granger Causality
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to causal discovery from streaming data, addressing the limitations of traditional methods that necessitate static datasets. The core of the proposed algorithm combines Bayesian Networks with Granger causality tests to effectively learn causal relationships from dynamic data streams. The algorithm iteratively updates the Bayesian network structure based on Granger causality results, providing a robust mechanism for adapting to changing relationships within the stream. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical framework and illustrate its potential applications in real-time system monitoring and dynamic decision-making. The key contribution lies in the integration of two distinct yet complementary techniques, enabling causal discovery in environments where data arrives continuously and evolves over time. The algorithm's ability to handle temporal dependencies and adapt to evolving relationships makes it particularly suitable for complex, real-world streaming data scenarios.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Causal Discovery from Streaming Data
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of causal discovery from streaming data, a scenario where complete datasets are typically unavailable. Traditional causal discovery methods rely on observing the entire dataset simultaneously, a constraint that severely limits their applicability in dynamic and evolving environments. We propose a novel approach utilizing Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) to incrementally learn causal relationships from a continuous stream of data. The algorithm adapts to changes in the underlying data distribution, providing a robust and efficient solution for causal inference in streaming scenarios. The core of our method lies in maintaining a probabilistic representation of the causal structure through a DBN, updating it continuously as new data arrives. We detail the learning process, including Bayesian inference, parameter estimation, and structure learning, specifically designed for the characteristics of streaming data. The adaptive nature of the DBN allows it to capture evolving causal relationships, offering a significant advantage over static causal discovery approaches. This work presents a practical framework for causal discovery in real-world streaming data applications, where timely and accurate causal understanding is paramount.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery via Latent Variable Dynamics in Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery within dynamic Bayesian networks, specifically addressing the challenges posed by latent variables and feedback loops. Existing causal discovery algorithms often struggle to accurately model these complex systems, leading to inaccurate inferences. Our method extends Bayesian network learning by integrating latent variables, represented through Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), into the learning process. We leverage variational inference and approximate inference techniques to manage the computational complexity arising from the inclusion of latent variables and the modeling of feedback loops. The core innovation lies in the dynamic adaptation of the Bayesian network structure, allowing it to evolve alongside the underlying system dynamics. We demonstrate, theoretically and conceptually, the benefits of this approach, focusing on improved accuracy and robustness compared to traditional methods when dealing with systems exhibiting significant latent variable influence and cyclical relationships. The ultimate goal is to provide a more reliable framework for uncovering causal relationships in complex, real-world scenarios.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Causal Discovery from Observational Data
papers.abstract: Causal discovery aims to infer causal relationships from observational data, a critical task in fields ranging from medicine to economics. Traditional approaches often rely on conditional independence tests, which struggle to accurately represent complex, non-linear relationships, particularly in high-dimensional datasets. This paper introduces a novel framework utilizing Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) to address these limitations. The core idea is to evolve a Bayesian network structure over time, explicitly incorporating temporal dependencies present in sequential observational data. We propose a new Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method designed for efficient inference within the evolving DBN structure. The resulting model offers a more robust and accurate representation of causal relationships compared to static conditional independence methods. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through theoretical analysis and outline key considerations for implementation. The primary contribution lies in providing a dynamic, time-aware approach to causal discovery, mitigating the pitfalls of traditional static methods.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery via Observational Data with Dynamic Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to causal discovery utilizing Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs). Traditional causal discovery methods often struggle with datasets exhibiting temporal dependencies and feedback loops, leading to inaccurate or incomplete causal models. This work addresses this limitation by constructing DBNs that explicitly represent these dynamic relationships. The core of the method lies in employing algorithms such as PC to learn the structure of the DBN from observational data, carefully incorporating time-varying covariates and feedback effects. The resulting DBN provides a more nuanced and accurate representation of causal relationships compared to static causal models. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline its potential for applications in domains where temporal dynamics play a crucial role in understanding causal mechanisms. The key innovation lies in the dynamic nature of the network, enabling the capture of evolving causal influences.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery via Structural Equation Modeling with Bayesian Networks and Granger Causality
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to causal discovery that addresses the limitations of existing algorithms, particularly their vulnerability to confounding variables. The core idea is to integrate Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), Bayesian Networks, and Granger causality tests into a unified framework. SEM provides a theoretical foundation for defining causal relationships, Bayesian Networks capture conditional dependencies between variables, and Granger causality tests are employed to detect temporal dependencies indicative of causal influence. The combination of these techniques offers a more robust and accurate method for inferring causal relationships from observational data. We demonstrate the potential of this multi-faceted approach through a theoretical discussion and outline a potential implementation strategy. The key contribution lies in the synergistic application of these diverse techniques, enhancing the reliability of causal inference in complex scenarios. This work aims to improve upon current causal discovery methodologies by incorporating temporal and network-based information alongside traditional SEM formulations.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery from Observational Data using Bayesian Networks with Intervention Simulations
papers.abstract: Inferring causal relationships from observational data is a fundamental problem in statistics and artificial intelligence. Traditional methods often struggle with confounding, where observed correlations between variables mask true causal connections. This paper proposes a novel approach to causal discovery that leverages Bayesian networks and intervention simulations. The core idea is to simulate interventions within the Bayesian network structure to directly observe the effects of manipulating variables and thereby mitigate confounding bias. We formulate the problem as estimating a causal Bayesian network structure where intervention effects are explicitly incorporated into the learning process. This approach offers a more robust way to identify causal relationships compared to standard observational data analysis. The methodology is presented, and the theoretical underpinnings are discussed, highlighting the key contributions and potential improvements. The paper focuses on the algorithmic aspects and theoretical considerations, offering a framework for future research in this area.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery from High-Dimensional Observational Data via Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for causal discovery from high-dimensional observational data leveraging Bayesian Networks. The core challenge in causal discovery is the "curse of dimensionality," where the complexity of the data rapidly increases with the number of variables, leading to inaccurate and incomplete causal graphs. Existing algorithms frequently fail to scale effectively or introduce significant biases in high-dimensional settings. Our approach incorporates prior knowledge through expert-defined constraints and utilizes regularization techniques to mitigate the impact of noise and redundancy. The algorithm iteratively refines a Bayesian Network structure by evaluating conditional independence tests, incorporating prior probabilities, and applying a penalty term that favors simpler, more parsimonious graphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the method through theoretical analysis and illustrative examples, highlighting its ability to generate more reliable causal structures compared to traditional methods in high-dimensional scenarios. The key contribution lies in a robust framework that balances exploration of potential causal relationships with the need for structural simplicity, ultimately providing a more accurate representation of the underlying causal mechanisms.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery from Observational Data using Deep Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery from observational data by leveraging deep Bayesian networks. Traditional causal discovery methods often rely on strong assumptions or require expert knowledge, limiting their applicability in complex scenarios. This research addresses this limitation by employing deep neural networks to learn the conditional independence structure directly from data. The core idea is to train a deep Bayesian network, essentially a neural network, to capture the underlying dependencies between variables, thereby inferring causal relationships. We demonstrate that this data-driven approach can effectively uncover causal connections even in the absence of prior knowledge, offering a powerful tool for analyzing complex datasets and generating causal hypotheses. The proposed methodology provides a significant advancement in causal discovery, bridging the gap between data-driven learning and causal inference. The key components include a deep neural network architecture designed for learning conditional independence, a training objective that encourages accurate representation of the data's dependencies, and a method for extracting the learned Bayesian network from the trained neural network. The resulting Bayesian network provides a probabilistic representation of the causal relationships, which can then be used for various downstream tasks, such as prediction, intervention analysis, and causal explanation. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential limitations and future directions of this research.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Causal Discovery from Observational Data using Bayesian Networks with Dynamic Structure Learning
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to causal discovery from observational data utilizing dynamic Bayesian networks. Traditional Bayesian network structure learning methods often assume static datasets, failing to capture evolving causal relationships encountered in dynamic environments. Our methodology addresses this limitation by incorporating a dynamic structure learning algorithm that continuously adapts the Bayesian network's topology and parameter estimates as new data streams arrive. We leverage a variational inference technique to efficiently maintain probabilistic representations throughout this adaptation process. The core innovation lies in the iterative refinement of the network structure, allowing it to accurately represent causal dependencies that may shift over time. This approach offers a robust solution for causal discovery in scenarios where the underlying data distribution is not stationary, a common characteristic of many real-world applications. The system is designed to provide a more accurate understanding of causal relationships compared to static Bayesian network approaches, significantly improving decision-making capabilities in dynamic systems. The presented method is scalable and can handle large datasets, offering a practical solution for complex causal inference problems.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Discovery of interconnected causal drivers of COVID-19 vaccination intentions in the US using a causal Bayesian network
papers.abstract: Holistic interventions to overcome COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy require a system-level understanding of the interconnected causes and mechanisms that give rise to it. However, conventional correlative analyses do not easily provide such nuanced insights. We used an unsupervised, hypothesis-free causal discovery algorithm to learn the interconnected causal pathways to vaccine intention as a causal Bayesian network (BN), using data from a COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy survey in the US in early 2021. We identified social responsibility, vaccine safety and anticipated regret as prime candidates for interventions and revealed a complex network of variables that mediate their influences. Social responsibility's causal effect greatly exceeded that of other variables. The BN revealed that the causal impact of political affiliations was weak compared with more direct causal factors. This approach provides clearer targets for intervention than regression, suggesting it can be an effective way to explore multiple causal pathways of complex behavioural problems to inform interventions.

papers.title: A guide to bayesian networks software for structure and parameter learning, with a focus on causal discovery tools
papers.abstract: A representation of the cause-effect mechanism is needed to enable artificial intelligence to represent how the world works. Bayesian Networks (BNs) have proven to be an effective and versatile tool for this task. BNs require constructing a structure of dependencies among variables and learning the parameters that govern these relationships. These tasks, referred to as structural learning and parameter learning, are actively investigated by the research community, with several algorithms proposed and no single method having established itself as standard. A wide range of software, tools, and packages have been developed for BNs analysis and made available to academic researchers and industry practitioners. As a consequence of having no one-size-fits-all solution, moving the first practical steps and getting oriented into this field is proving to be challenging to outsiders and beginners. In this paper, we review the most relevant tools and software for BNs structural and parameter learning to date, with a focus on causal discovery tools, providing our subjective recommendations directed to an audience of beginners. In addition, we provide an extensive easy-to-consult overview table summarizing all software packages and their main features. By improving the reader's understanding of which available software might best suit their needs, we improve accessibility to the field and make it easier for beginners to take their first step into it.

papers.title: Causal Discovery via Simulation-Based Bayesian Networks with Latent Action Models
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery, leveraging simulation-based Bayesian Networks (SBNs) augmented with latent action models. Traditional causal discovery algorithms often fail when dealing with complex, high-dimensional systems influenced by unobserved actions – a common scenario in real-world applications. The core idea is to simulate the system under various action scenarios, generating synthetic data that incorporates the effects of these latent actions. This simulated data is then used within a Bayesian Network framework to infer causal relationships.
